source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Avoid every cephalosporin permanently, because any penicillin allergy creates the same high cross-reactivity with all agents.","B":"Assess the prior reaction and specific cephalosporin; later-generation agents generally have low IgE cross-reactivity.","C":"Administer without taking an allergy history, because penicillin and cephalosporin reactions are completely unrelated.","D":"Use cephalosporins after severe delayed penicillin reactions without review, because non-IgE reactions pose no concern."}}
source_row.rationale: Cephalosporin use after a penicillin allergy depends on the specific prior reaction and cephalosporin. Later-generation agents have low IgE cross-reactivity, while severe delayed beta-lactam reactions warrant avoidance/specialist guidance.
source_row.source_detail: Cross-reactivity section: third-generation cephalosporins have lower cross-reactivity with IgE-mediated penicillin allergy (<1%) than first/second generation; severe non-IgE reactions require different management. CDC STI Treatment Guidelines penicillin-allergy page, current guidance rechecked 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: CDC — Penicillin Allergy and Cephalosporin Cross-Reactivity
source_row.stem: A client reports a prior penicillin allergy and is prescribed a cephalosporin. Which assessment principle is most accurate?
